claims.text: The interviewer records his own reservations inside the document. Of the propulsion explanation: '[note: think he's talking frequency here, not wavelength, but he continued to confuse the two; also, long antenna hardly consistent with detecting extremely hi freq, if that's really what he meant.]' Of the witness's terms, in notes written 'after leaving meeting, while driving': 'He reminded me a couple of times that he gets $200/hr. as a designer. So, who knows--he may charge us. he also said if we wanted a good rendering of the base burning vehicle, he could provide that for a couple thousand dollars.'

claims.text: The document contains the witness disowning part of McCandlish's drawing. Shown the sketches, Sorensen says of the manned vehicle: 'this is probably the farthest from what I saw, and no, I didn't see anything with an intake up above the windows like this', and 'mark extrapolates a bit too much'. Of the saucer drawing he says the opposite: 'you've got a drawing, as accurate as I could get [the round, saucer-looking thing]. This dwg is so GD..accurate that I can't be much more specific than this.'

desc: This is the strongest artefact in the whole thread and it cuts both ways. It is a contemporaneous working file authored by a named trade-press editor within two years of the claimed event: thirty-one scanned pages, opening with handwritten notes on Aviation Week & Space Technology letterhead over the name block 'William B. Scott / Senior Engineering Editor', followed by a sixteen page typed transcript headed 'NOTES FROM INTERVIEW ON 12-3-90 WITH BRAD' and 'COMPILED 12-11-90; SCOTT/AVWK LANCASTER'. It carries the claim in the witness's own words, and it carries the interviewer's own doubts in the same pages: a bracketed note that the witness 'continued to confuse' frequency and wavelength, and a note written while driving away that the witness had twice mentioned his $200 an hour rate and had offered a rendering for 'a couple thousand dollars'. Nothing in the thirty-one pages is a published article. Aviation Week printed McCandlish's artwork, not this interview. The scan reached the public through an anonymously operated website in December 2024 and its custody before that date is not established by anything in it.

unverified: That William B. Scott was a test pilot at Edwards Air Force Base in the early 1970s, as McCandlish's 2001 testimony states. Not opened. What IS opened is his masthead title, 'Senior Engineering Editor', on the 1990 letterhead.

Scott's alleged motive for not publishing. research/leads/gerb-corpus-25-35.md file 33 at 00;22;44 and 00;30;16 records UAP Gerb reading Scott's stated reason as disbelief. That reading was not verified: Scott's reservations inside the document are about the witness's physics and about his fee, and the document contains no stated refusal to publish.

The Aviation Week & Space Technology issue of 1 October 1990, in which the document says McCandlish's paintings of two aircraft appeared, was not opened. The year 1990 follows only from the document's own December 1990 dating.
